intuition.text: Moss, a gallery patrol robot, keeps walking while its facing drifts. Each update remembers the previous facing and adds a small signed turn. That memory gives the trail continuity: choosing an entirely new compass direction would make each update unrelated to the last.
intuition.situation: Use this when an idle character should roam without a destination and its movement system accepts velocity directly. It gives Moss motion to watch; it does not give the patrol a route or a guarantee of visiting every room.

example.name: Moss patrols an empty gallery
example.description: Moss starts at ({startX}, {startY}), facing {startHeading} radians, and immediately walks at {speed} units/s. Every {timeStep} s it draws a signed turn rate bounded by {maxRotation} radians/s. Seed {seed} makes the {duration}-second patrol replayable. The comparison raises only the turn-rate bound to {failureRotation} radians/s. The empty gallery has no walls or stopping rule.

steps.title: Read the current facing as velocity
steps.text: Convert the remembered angle with the public engine's deterministic cosine and sine, normalise the direction and multiply by {speed}. Moss uses this velocity immediately; there is no acceleration ramp. The green arrow is this update's displacement direction.

steps.title: Draw a small signed turn
steps.text: Take the difference of successive uniform draws. Small differences are more common than extreme ones; the sign chooses a turning direction. Multiplying by {maxRotation} gives a turn rate. The seeded generator is study-local because the engine's random helpers are not public exports.

steps.title: Move, then remember the new facing
steps.text: Move with the velocity calculated from the old facing, then add turnRate × {timeStep} to that facing. The amber arrow previews the next update's velocity. This direct kinematic update is study-local: the public engine's wander function is an acceleration-based behaviour with a forward circle, a different mechanism.

pseudocode.ordinary:
direction = normalize({ x: cosine(heading), y: sine(heading) })
velocity = direction * speed

[first, seed] = seededUniform(seed)
[second, seed] = seededUniform(seed)
sample = first - second
turnRate = sample * maxRotation

position = position + velocity * timeStep
heading = heading + turnRate * timeStep
remember(position, heading, seed)

visual.textEquivalent: At {seconds} s, Moss is at ({x}, {y}), facing {heading} radians and moving at {currentSpeed} units/s; the green velocity is ({velocityX}, {velocityY}), {turnDescription}, and the amber next-update direction faces {nextHeading} radians.

implementations.project: AI Steering Behaviors for Games · KinematicWander.cs
implementations.relevance: This public C# teaching collection supplies Unity components for classic movement behaviours. Its kinematic wander component exposes speed, rotation range and separate waiting periods for turning and translation.
implementations.explanation: RandomBinomial subtracts two floating-point uniform draws. Separate coroutines set rotation and translate along the object's forward vector. Rotation is assigned as an absolute Euler angle rather than accumulated, and translation is a distance per coroutine iteration without elapsed-time scaling. Those choices make its clocks and units part of its behaviour; the file is an implementation to inspect, with limits visible in its code.

references.title: AI for Games, third edition · Chapter 3 Movement · 3.2.2 Wandering
references.supports: Identifies the book whose coverage of this topic the supplied catalog places at Chapter 3, section 3.2.2 Wandering. DOI content negotiation confirmed bibliographic metadata; chapter text was not read.

references.title: KinematicWander.cs · pinned public Unity implementation
references.supports: The component subtracts two uniform draws and uses separate rotation and forward-translation coroutines, with absolute rotation assignment and no elapsed-time factor in its translation call.

limits: A large turn-rate bound can make consecutive velocities point more than a right angle apart while speed stays unchanged. Raising it to {failureRotation} in the comparison exposes this abrupt change: the mechanism imposes no limit on acceleration or turning acceleration.
Moss has no knowledge of gallery walls, other visitors or patrol coverage. A smooth-looking trail is not evidence of safe movement or an effective patrol.
The draw rate is part of the model. Changing {timeStep} changes both how often Moss samples and how far each sample turns it, so a different update rate does not preserve the same random walk.

nearby.why: Open Random binomial to examine why the two-draw difference favours smaller turns and how its sampling affects the path.
Use Wander when the movement system needs bounded acceleration toward a changing point ahead instead of replacing velocity directly.
Use Path following when Moss must inspect a prescribed route; random wandering offers no coverage guarantee.
